19724-home-pastimes-or-tableaux-vivants:
Tableaux vivants are living pictures: costumed people holding still as famous scenes. J. H. Head's Home Pastimes teaches families how to stage them at home. The book opens on the nature of a perfect picture. It claims such pictures are appreciated wherever they are shown. Poetic feeling, it argues, shows itself the same way everywhere.

Parlor entertainment mattered before radio filled the evenings. A good tableau needed costumes, poses, curtains, and nerve. Head gives home players the craft behind the trick. Readers learn how Victorian families amused their guests. The book also preserves period taste in scenes and dress. It is a handbook from the age of the drawing-room stage.
19860-the-arabian-nights-entertainments:
The Arabian Nights Entertainments gathers the tales of the Thousand and One Nights. This 1914 edition traces the collection's deep roots. Tenth-century Arabic writers already mention a Persian book called The Thousand Nights. In it, Scheherazade wins one more day of life with each tale. Many stories show Persian or Hindu origins beneath Arabic dress. Aladdin, Sindbad, and Ali Baba live in this tradition.

No single author made the Nights; centuries of tellers did. Frame story, genies, and Baghdad streets bind hundreds of tales. English readers met them through many translations and selections. The collection shaped Western dreams of the East profoundly. It also preserves folk tales of real antiquity. Every edition is a door into that shared story-hoard.
19870-illuminated-manuscripts:
Illuminated Manuscripts introduces the art of hand-decorated books. It begins from a broad claim: the desire for decoration is as old as the human race. Nature is the source of beauty, the author argues. Something in us reproduces felt beauty in material form. That reproduction may appeal to eye or ear. Medieval gold-leaf pages are the book's great exhibit.

John W. Bradley wrote standard handbooks on medieval art crafts. Illumination joined painting, calligraphy, and goldsmith work in one page. This guide explains styles, pigments, and famous examples. It served the Victorian revival of manuscript arts. Kelmscott Press designs drew on the same love. The book remains a friendly doorway into the scriptorium.
19978-35-sonnets:
Fernando Pessoa wrote his 35 Sonnets in English, publishing them in Lisbon in 1918. One sonnet here thinks on a long-dead beloved. The speaker could not think of her as mere rotted dust. She had been long dead, yet lived entire in his seeing thought. What she was in him had never fled, he insists. The argument turns grief into metaphysics in fourteen lines.

Pessoa, Portugal's great modernist, wrote under many invented authors, called heteronyms. The sonnets are signed with his own name yet feel Shakespeare-haunted. Their English is deliberately archaic and knotted. Readers watch a Portuguese genius wrestle English tradition itself. These thirty-five poems are small, dense, and strange. They reward the slowest possible reading.
20161-sophisms-of-the-protectionists:
Sophisms of the Protectionists attacks the case for tariffs that guard home trade. A sophism is a slick argument that sounds true but is not. Free traders offered this small book at the cost of printing. They urged each reader to hand a copy to protectionist friends.

That push shows how hot the tariff fight ran in its day. Cheap imports, jobs, and prices all hung on the debate then. The book answers guard-trade claims point by point in plain words. Readers get a neat fossil of a fight that still echoes in trade politics.
20176-the-drone-a-play-in-three-acts:
Rutherford Mayne wrote The Drone, a play in three acts, published in 1912. An elderly man with a gloomy face enters a kitchen slowly. Sly humor in his eyes relieves that gloom at once. He looks at Kate, then scans the dresser with a disgusted shake.

Mayne wrote Irish plays that mix rural talk with sharp character study. A drone, in hive terms, is one who lives off others' work. That charge hangs over the men in this kitchen drama. Readers get Ulster speech, family friction, and humor with a sting in it.
20177-john-bull-or-the-englishman-s-fire:
George Colman the Younger wrote John Bull, a comedy in five acts, for the English stage. Colman defends true comedy against the pull of broad farce. Farce, he argues, has trained crowds to love hearty laughter alone. Smiles, by contrast, are now scorned as weak and insipid fare.

John Bull stands for the plain Englishman in this lively play. Colman sought a picture from real life, not mere caricature on stage. His comedy turns on money, class, and bluster in English homes. Readers get Georgian theatre with wit aimed at national pride itself.
20217-the-stranger-a-drama-in-five-acts:
The Stranger is a drama in five acts, a stage play of faith and doubt. Its preface warns how sacred faith is often badly taught in schools. Pious but ignorant teaching can breed the very doubts it fears. Infidelity may be sown where teachers meant to root it out.

Such a charge sets a grave tone for the drama that follows. A stranger's arrival in plays of this kind often tests a whole town. Belief, love, and hidden pasts tend to collide around such a figure. Readers get a serious period drama on faith taught well or ill.
20450-the-lives-of-the-fathers-martyrs-a:
The Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs, and Other Principal Saints is the great English collection of saints' lives, first made by Alban Butler. This edition adds lives written since the author's death. It aims to give readers a saint for study across the whole church year.

The editors worked to render the collection as complete as possible. They added the life of Saint Alphonsus Liguori and other saints canonized after Butler died, lives found in no earlier form of the work. Generations of Catholic readers used these volumes for daily devotion and for the stories behind feast days.
20537-the-argonauts: The Argonauts takes its title from the old seekers of the golden fleece and applies it to modern hunters of wealth. Its pages describe men working options and exchanges in many markets and corporations. Such men, the book says, need opposite qualities at once. They need the courage of the lion, the caution of the fox, and the talons of the falcon.
20543-edward-fitzgerald-and-posh-herring:
James Blyth's Edward FitzGerald and Posh tells the story of a strange friendship. FitzGerald, the poet of Omar Khayyam, grew close to Joseph Fletcher, a Lowestoft herring merchant nicknamed Posh. Blyth prints their connection and letters for the first time.

With the exception of Charles Lamb, Blyth writes, no man's letters have endeared his memory to so many readers. But the letters published before were written to cultured gentlemen, men of FitzGerald's own world. Posh was different: a working merchant of the herring fleet. The book shows the poet's warmth across the barriers of class.
20755-short-studies-on-great-subjects:
History, says the voice in Short Studies on Great Subjects, can look like a child's box of letters. We pick the letters we like, spell the word we want, and hide the rest. That sharp image opens a set of essays on grand themes.

James Anthony Froude, the famed historian, wrote studies of this kind with bold sweep. Faith, rule, sea power, and great lives pass under his gaze. He writes as a thinker, not a mere keeper of facts. Readers who like strong views in fine prose will find his essays both grand in scope and open to sharp debate.
20989-a-comedy-of-errors-in-seven-acts:
Tyrants crush distant isles and bend a worthy race under a foreign yoke, this verse drama cries. A noble charge waits within thy grasp, its speaker urges in high, old tones. A Comedy of Errors in Seven Acts speaks in that grave stage dress.

Verse, tyranny, and a helpless people's plea mark this odd, earnest play. Its seven acts promise error and tangle on a grand scale. Little is known of its stage life beyond its printed page. The book stands as a curio of amateur drama, where lofty verse and bold claims far outrun the footlights it likely never met.
21211-silverpoints:
John Gray's Silverpoints is a slim book of delicate, highly wrought poems. Elkin Mathews and John Lane published it in London in 1893 at the Bodley Head. Many carry French dedications and titles. The opening piece follows courtly ladies through an orchard, bending under low, forked branches over dew-soaked grass.

Gray was linked with the decadent writers of the 1890s, and these poems favour rare words, fine images, and slow, languid movement. A poem to Paul Verlaine appears among them. In the printed book the verse was set in italics, a design flourish this text edition notes but cannot show. Silverpoints remains Gray's best-known collection.
21253-the-swedish-norwegian-union-crisis:
K. Nordlund published this history with documents at Uppsala and Stockholm in 1905, the year Norway broke its union with Sweden. He promises a condensed account of the last few years plus extracts from the key documents. The consular question, whether Norway could have its own consuls, sits at the centre of the quarrel.

Nordlund writes from the Swedish side, answering a brochure by Fridtjof Nansen and accusing Norwegian agitation of mishandling plain facts. He traces the crisis back to the union's founding in 1814. Read today, the book shows how a constitutional dispute over trade officials nearly brought two kingdoms to war.
21396-the-three-lieutenants:
Three young officers of the Royal Navy meet again in W. H. G. Kingston's The Three Lieutenants. The book is the second in a set that begins with The Three Midshipmen. It shows life in the navy of the 1860s, when the three friends now hold higher rank.

By a happy chance, their postings let them serve near each other once more. Old Admiral Triton, now retired, still follows their careers with pride. Kingston first won fame with these books, which came out in weekly parts. Sea service, friendship, and fresh adventure fill this long tale, which ends with The Three Admirals.
21401-in-new-granada-or-heroes-and-patri:
South America's wars for freedom from Spain form the ground of W. H. G. Kingston's In New Granada. The narrator's father came from an old Covenanter family in Dumfriesshire, one of six sons. Most of those sons had to seek their luck in the wide world.

English folk are caught up in the fight of the Patriots against Spanish rule. The tale shows camp, march, and clash across a whole small country. Kingston sides with the cause of freedom, and he draws the Spanish as harsh foes. Travel, battle, and close escapes carry the story from one end of the land to the other.
21442-your-plants:
James Sheehan gives plain help for home growers in Your Plants, first entered for copyright in 1884. The full title promises care of tender and hardy plants in house and garden. The idea came to Sheehan at a large meeting of florists in western New York.

Early chapters treat lawns, potting soils, bought feeds, and the sowing of seeds. Later ones cover watering, winter storage in cellars, and the law of colour in flowers. Sheehan also explains layering, cuttings, and grafting in short, clear steps. The Orange Judd reprint of 1919 kept the book in reach of home gardeners.
21515-venice-preserved-a-tragedy-in-five:
Thomas Otway's Venice Preserved, a tragedy in five acts, is given here in an 1874 acting edition. Dio Boucicault revised the text for Booth's Theatre, with stage business, casts, and dress lists. Jaffier, Pierre, and Belvidera wear rich Venetian garb, down to plumes and rosettes.

The play turns on a plot against the senate of Venice and a friend torn two ways. Jaffier must choose between his fellow plotters and the wife he loves. The preface notes how Otway built a great work from a few thin facts of history. Few English tragedies of his age have held the stage so well.
21531-woodwork-joints:
Woodwork Joints, in the Woodworker series, teaches how joints are set out, made, and used. Four hundred pictures back the text, and an index closes the revised edition. The editor calls the range of joints unmatched in any prior book of its kind.

Teachers of handicraft get exercises of real use for class work at every level. The book treats the two secrets of good building: knowing how, and knowing why. Companion volumes in the series cover tools, staining, turning, and carving. For home workers and pros alike, the joint is where craft stands or falls, and this guide takes it joint by joint.
21570-the-squire-an-original-comedy-in-t:
Arthur W. Pinero's comedy The Squire first played at the St James's Theatre on December 29, 1881. This edition, copyrighted in 1905, prints the cast of that first night. Mrs Kendal played Kate Verity, and Mr Kendal played Lieutenant Thorndyke.

The scene is a decayed, weather-beaten Elizabethan mansion, ivy over broken stone. A secret marriage drives the first act, in a village of clergy, officers, gossips, and watchful kin. A reporter from the Pagley Mercury pokes into local affairs. Pinero, then a rising playwright, mixes romance, family secrets, and village comedy in three neat, well-made acts.
21583-children-of-the-tenements:
Jacob A. Riis tells tales of New York's poorest children in Children of the Tenements, copyrighted in 1897 and issued in 1903. Riis had written How the Other Half Lives and The Battle with the Slum. Pictures by C. M. Relyea and others show the world he describes.

Adam Grunschlag sits at his street stand in falling snow, lost in thought. Around him the holiday bustle grows, and he heeds none of it. Story by story, Riis shows barefoot kids in passageways and families crammed in dark rooms. His tales plead, without preaching, for the children the rich city forgot.
21820-oh-susannah-a-farcical-comedy-in-t:
A doctor's consulting room in Pimlico is the single scene of Oh! Susannah!, a farcical comedy in three acts by Mark Ambient. The play ran first at the Eden Theatre, Brighton, in September 1897, then at the Royalty in London. Its action is continuous, from four to six on a Lady Day afternoon. The three acts take under two hours in the playing.

The printed text gives the full stage world: whiskey decanter, medical chest, surgical knives, microscope, and a detective camera shaped like a turnip watch. Farce needs its props, and Ambient lists them all. The dialogue runs in servants' slang and drawing-room polish. It is a tidy relic of the light London stage of the 1890s.
21849-the-mind-the-paint-girl-a-comedy-i:
London's smart set talks, flirts, and schemes in The Mind the Paint Girl, a comedy in four acts by Arthur Wing Pinero, published in 1912. The cast list alone tells the story's world. A viscount, a colonel, and a German baron mix with an actress's manager and a crowd of young men about town. Pinero's name heads a long shelf of stage hits, from The Second Mrs. Tanqueray to Trelawny of the Wells.

The title comes from a warning cry in painters' studios, turned here toward a girl of the stage. Pinero builds his comedy on manners, money, and the fear of a wet-paint reputation. The printed play keeps the third-act song in full. It shows the master of the well-made play near the end of his reign.
21865-king-arthur-and-his-knights:
Arthur pulls the sword and gathers his knights in Maude L. Radford's King Arthur and His Knights, published at Chicago in 1903. Walter J. Enright's pictures show the king, the Round Table, and the Holy Grail. The tales run in order: Arthur made king, Excalibur won, Guinevere wed, and Gareth come to court unknown. Lancelot, Balin, Geraint, and Enid each take their turn at the center.

Radford retells the old legends in clear prose pitched to young readers. The search for the Holy Grail and the death of Arthur close the book, as they must. She keeps the wonder and trims the tangle. For many American children, this was the first door into Camelot, and it opens easily still.
21928-light-freights:
A night-watchman on a wharf holds court in W. W. Jacobs's Light Freights, a book of comic tales from 1901. Speaking of money, the watchman says, the world would be brighter if we all had more of it. Then he admits that being short sharpens people, and tells of the sharpest man he ever knew, who never had a ha'penny. That voice, thoughtful and sly, frames tale after tale.

The stories bear titles like Hard Labour, A Garden Plot, and The Resurrection of Mr. Wiggett. Jacobs peoples them with sailors, skippers, and schemers along the Thames. His dialogue, thick with dropped aitches, carries the comedy. Light Freights is Jacobs in his prime form: short, dry tales where human nature is the cargo and folly pays the freight.
21932-embarrassments:
Four long tales by Henry James make up Embarrassments, published in 1896, and each turns on a delicate social or artistic knot. The Figure in the Carpet opens the book: a young critic is set to review Hugh Vereker's new novel for The Middle. His friend Corvick came breathless with the task, and the critic pounces on the advance copy. Inside Vereker's work hides a secret figure, and the hunt for it drives the tale.

Glasses, The Next Time, and The Way It Came follow, studies of sight, failure, and return. James writes of writers and their readers with a surgeon's calm. The title is exact: everyone here is caught in some fine, painful awkwardness. These are among his most perfect shorter works, built from talk, glances, and the things people cannot say.
21936-theft-a-play-in-four-acts:
Washington power and a stolen document drive Jack London's play Theft, written in 1910 and set across twenty hours in the capital. Senator Chalmers's wife Margaret stands at the center: twenty-seven, intellectual, womanly, and capable of sudden hardness. Against her father's house stands Howard Knox, a congressman from Oregon with a vision he has followed through abuse and ridicule. The magnate Anthony Starkweather, Margaret's father, holds the purse of the piece.

London, the novelist of the Klondike and the sea, turns to the stage with a socialist's brief. Labor agitators, embassy secretaries, and ministers crowd his cast list. The theft of the title is both a crime and an accusation about wealth itself. It is a fiery, talky period play, more argued than acted in its afterlife.
22112-a-child-s-book-of-saints:
William Canton retold the lives of the saints for young readers in A Child's Book of Saints. Canton, a poet and historian of the Bible Society, had a gift for simple, musical English. His saints are presented as friends and heroes for children to love. Martyrs, hermits, kings, and maidens appear in short, clear chapters.

Each life stresses a single virtue: courage, patience, charity, or faith under scorn. Canton avoids both gore and dryness, keeping wonder in the tales. The book came from an age when saints' stories were standard nursery reading across Britain. It remains a graceful sample of Victorian and Edwardian religious writing for the young.
22293-three-margarets:
Laura E. Richards, daughter of Julia Ward Howe, published Three Margarets in 1897 for girl readers. A pleasant summer rain opens the book, plashing on elms and locusts and tinkling in roadside puddles. On the roof of a great landau rolling toward Fernley House the rain drums less musically. Inside, three girls ride buried in their own thoughts, and each of them is Margaret.

Cousins with one name and three temperaments must live together for a season. Richards builds the story from their contrasts, quarrels, and reconciliations. Her girls' books were famous for sense and humour without preaching. Three Margarets is a gentle specimen, written in her mother's long shadow and her own clear voice.
22314-mysticism-and-its-results:
Mysticism and Its Results is a short book that gathers facts outside the usual range of reading. Its writer asks for the reader's patience at the start. The essay, he says, is suggestive rather than didactic.

That modesty sets the book's method and aim. It does not claim to settle its subject once for all. Instead, it hopes to induce thought, study, or research in honest minds. If it does only that, the writer says, its object will be attained. Readers get an invitation rather than a lecture: a small, earnest case that mystical experience deserves serious, open attention.
22485-devon-its-moorlands-streams-and-co:
Lady Rosalind Northcote wrote Devon: Its Moorlands, Streams, and Coasts. Her book guides readers through England's great western county. Even its opening quotes Shakespeare on Exeter's old castle, Rougemont.

When last at Exeter, the quoted lines run, the mayor showed the castle. He called it Rougemont, at which name the speaker started. An Irish bard had warned he would not live long after seeing Richmond. Such lore flavors Northcote's tour of her home county. Moorland, stream, and coast each get their chapters of attention. Readers get Edwardian local writing at its proudest. Devon appears as history, scenery, and home ground together.
22685-the-classification-of-patents:
The Classification of Patents is a treatise on how patent offices sort inventions into classes so that examiners and inventors can find what came before. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Behind the dry title stands a real problem: hundreds of thousands of patents, useless unless a searcher can find the right shelf.

The author begins at the root: classification lies at the foundation of all mental process. Without seeing resemblances and differences, and grouping things by them, judgment itself is impossible, and reason cannot move from the known to the unknown. From that philosophy the book descends to bins, subclasses, and search practice. It will interest students of information science, who may recognize an early theory of their own field wearing legal dress.
22784-on-laboratory-arts:
Richard Threlfall wrote On Laboratory Arts, a handbook of the mechanical skills behind experimental physics. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Threlfall, an Australian physicist, held that great experiments rest on humble crafts: glassblowing, metalwork, vacuum pumps, and the making of things that cannot be bought.

Experimental work in physical science, he begins, rests in the end upon the mechanical arts. In a well-appointed laboratory the appeal to those arts is often indirect, and a student handed ready apparatus may irresistibly ignore the mechanical basis of the work. The book exists to cure that ignorance. Generations of researchers kept it by the bench, and it remains the classic statement that discovery is also a handicraft.
23173-how-the-raven-died-1902-from-wolfv:
Alfred Henry Lewis dresses two soldiers in How the Raven Died, dated 1902, from Wolfville Nights. This violent person in buckskins, the Old Cattleman says, is a second lieutenant, a mere boy, from West Point. While that outcast in the ridiculous hat is foaled on the plains and never does go that close to the rising sun as to glimpse the Old Missouri. Yet the pair, he swears, are as much alike as the far East is to itself.

Wolfville's narrator spins the tale in the Arizona camp's full dialect, buckskins, West Point, and an Indian called the Raven in one long breath. Lewis's Wolfville books made the mining-camp storyteller a national figure. The Raven's death gets told the camp way, sideways, through likenesses and lies, until the truth stands up in the firelight.
a-brief-bible-history-a-survey-of-the-ol:
A Brief Bible History, published in 1922 by James Oscar Boyd and J Gresham Machen, surveys the history of the Old and New Testaments. The book presents that history as the story of God's redeeming grace. Its chapters trace the stream of God's redeeming purposes flowing down through the older, Old Testament times.

The survey then follows the same purpose broadening and deepening in the New Testament, in Jesus Christ and his Church. Boyd and Machen wrote as Bible teachers, and the book reads as a clear, ordered introduction for students. It gives readers the whole arc of scripture in brief compass, from the first histories to the early church, in one connected account.
a-family-man-in-three-acts:
A Family Man is a play in three acts by John Galsworthy, published in 1922. Galsworthy was an English novelist and playwright, viewed as one of the first writers of the Edwardian era, who challenged the ideals of the society that Victorian literature before him had depicted. He later won the Nobel Prize for Literature, and his Forsyte Saga became his most famous work.

On stage, this play puts a family man at the center of domestic tension. Galsworthy's drama typically sets private comfort against public duty and respectability, and A Family Man works that ground in three acts. The printed play preserves a piece of his Edwardian theatre, from the years when his stage work stood beside his novels in reputation.
a-girl-among-the-anarchists: Isabel Meredith's novel takes a brave girl among the anarchists of London — the secret plots, the high ideals, the very real dangers of the movement. Written from inside knowledge, it thrills while it makes readers think. A rare window onto a shadowy, passionate world.
a-list-of-factorial-math-constants: This entry lists factorial-related mathematical constants. Numbers grow fast. The Tower library holds the full text. It counted huge. Products multiplied. Constants emerged. Math marveled. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
airship-wave-1896-1897-press-accounts:
Seventeen newspaper pieces from 1896 and 1897 make up The Great Airship Wave of 1896-1897, drawn from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America scans. Reports from Sacramento, Oakland, San Francisco, and San Jose open the scare in November 1896. By April 1897 the wave rolled over Kansas, Omaha, and Chicago, with inventors claiming the sky craft as their own.

Editors argued, witnesses swore, and hoaxers confessed in the columns reprinted here word for word. Nothing real was ever found, which makes the papers themselves the true record. The set preserves the primary evidence of America's first great mystery-airship panic, decades before flying saucers.
albertus-magnus-admirables-secrets:
Secrets ascribed to Albert the Great fill this French chapbook of natural magic, in a 1729 printing. Recipes, charms, and wonders of nature promise help with health, love, luck, and beasts. For two centuries it ranked among France's most popular books of hidden knowledge among common folk.

Herbs, stones, and household tricks mix with spells and signs in its pages. Scholars doubt the great Albert wrote a word of it himself. That hardly mattered to the buyers who treasured its lore. The book opens a window on popular belief, where folk magic and medieval science blend without a seam.
anthology-of-massachusetts-poets: William Braithwaite's anthology of Massachusetts poets: the Bay State's verse from colonial times to his own day. A valuable survey of New England poetry. For lovers of regional verse. Braithwaite's annual anthologies made him the dean of American poetry.
arizona-nights: Stewart Edward White's stories of the Arizona frontier, told around a campfire by a seasoned cattleman. Cowboys, prospectors, gunfights, and desert lore fill these yarns, written by a man who actually rode the range. Published in 1907, the book helped fix the image of the Southwest in the American imagination.
balfour-taoist-texts:
Frederic Henry Balfour gathered his Taoist Texts in English in 1884. His anthology sorts the writings by morals, rule, and deep thought. Victorian readers met the philosophy of the Way through books like this.

Short pieces from the Taoist tradition speak in Balfour's clear English. They teach softness over force, quiet rule, and scorn for mere show. Laozi's heirs prize the still mind above wealth and loud fame. Balfour's picks favor calm wisdom over magic and cult practice here. The book stands as an early Western window into Taoist thought and ethics. Its quiet counsel still speaks past its Victorian frame to readers.
beasts-and-super-beasts: Saki's 1914 Beasts and Super-Beasts satirizes Edwardian society with bite. Wit claws. The Tower library holds the full text. It beastly mocked. Society preened. Satire bit. Laughter cut. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
belinda-an-april-folly-in-three-acts: A. A. Milne — years before Winnie-the-Pooh — wrote this sparkling three-act comedy of an April folly that turns a respectable household upside down. Witty dialogue, romantic confusion, and Milne's light, deft touch fill an evening's entertainment. The play shows the future children's author as a sophisticated West End playwright at the height of his early powers.
brandes-eminent-authors-of-the-nineteent:
Brandes set aside his grand survey to write vivid portraits of leading nineteenth-century authors, gathered here in English. Many of his subjects were people he had met or known well. Memory and judgment mix in each sketch.

A portrait by Brandes is no dry summary of dates and books. He seeks the ruling passion of a mind and shows it at work. Praise and blame both come sharp and clear from his pen. The book pairs well with Main Currents, giving readers the critic as portrait painter, working from life as much as from the page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acceptants: This 1913 reference piece on the Acceptants — those who accepted the bull Unigenitus against Jansenism. Pierre Fournet tells their side. France's church split over the quarrel. Orthodoxy's party in a bitter fight. The quarrel outlived both its parties. Rome's thunder settled the matter at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adventists: A 1913 entry on the Adventists — the Millerite heirs who await Christ's return. Francis Havey explains their tenets. The Great Disappointment of 1844 shaped them. Seventh-day keepers form their largest body. An American-born movement. Their hospitals and schools circle the globe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-carpets: A 1913 entry on altar carpets — the sanctuary's woven floor. Augustin Schulte notes their modest use. Their patterns hush the footfall. The East loves them more than the West. A soft path to the holy. Their colors cheer the winter sanctuary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anabaptists: A 1913 entry on the Anabaptists — the rebaptizers of the Reformation. Nicholas Weber tells their turbulent tale. Münster's kingdom ended in blood. The Church condemned their errors. Zeal without the old order. Their descendants keep the quiet farms. Their hymns survive in the Ausbund.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustinians-: This 1913 reference piece on the Augustinians of the Assumption — d'Alzon's Assumptionists. Thomas Taaffe tells their worldwide work. Their press speaks in many tongues. The missions know their zeal. The order of the Assumption's sons. Their Bonne Presse prints the Paris dailies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bachelor-of-a: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on the Bachelor of Arts — the degree's medieval story. James Burns traces its scholastic roots. The trivium crowned the young scholar. The universities keep the old name. The first rung of the learned ladder. Its hood marks the graduate's rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptists: A 1913 entry on the Baptists — the brethren of the believer's baptism. Nicholas Weber tells their history. Their immersion divides them from Rome. The sects multiplied in the new world. A communion of the Reformation's children. Their churches dot the southern states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-adver: This 1913 reference piece on the Book of Advertisements — the Elizabethan church orders. Bernard Ward sets out its famous rules. Parker's injunctions shaped the settlement. The entry preserves its historic fame. The Advertisements of the new Church. Its vestments rule shaped the clergy's dress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-act: This 1913 reference piece on canonical acts — the Church's juridical deeds. Richard Burtsell sets out their solemn forms. The written record guards the rights. The chancery keeps their authentic texts. The jurisprudence of the Church's acts. Their rescripts bear the papal seal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-imp: A 1913 entry on canonical impediments — the bars to a valid marriage. Auguste Boudinhon unfolds their solemn list. Consanguinity and the prior bond. The dispensations ease the lesser bars. The law of the marriage bond. Their diriment bars void the bond.
