Two agents, one from the Drug Enforcement Administration and one from the Secret Service, became targets of corruption investigations tied to their work on the case. That twist made Silk Road a double story: a landmark cybercrime takedown and a warning about the temptations built into undercover work with digital money. Readers get the outline of the massive multi-agency hunt and the scandal that grew inside it, drawn from the released record.
hendershot-1928-press-accounts:
Lester Hendershot, an inventor from Pennsylvania, briefly stunned the press in 1928 with a motor that seemed to run on nothing. Six newspaper reports from that year are gathered here. Five come from the New York Times and one from the New York American, all from February and March.

The reports run from a test flight crowd that included Charles Lindbergh to the slow collapse of the claim. Backers from the Guggenheim fund soon backed away, and experts called the motor a trick. Read in order, the clippings show a free-energy sensation rising and dying in five weeks.
hobson-s-choice-a-lancashire-comedy-in-f: Harold Brighouse's beloved Lancashire comedy centers on Henry Hobson, a blustering Salford bootmaker who refuses to marry off his daughters. His eldest, Maggie, takes matters into her own hands: she marries Will Mossop, Hobson's best craftsman, and the pair open a rival shop across the street. First staged in 1915, the play's battle of wits between father and daughter still delights audiences.
imaginary-portraits: Pater paints lives that never were: a Dutch philosopher, a medieval martyr of art, and others. His prose is like carved ivory, cool and perfect. The finest stories of the aesthetic age, beautiful and sad.
island-nights-entertainments:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these three tales of the South Seas in his last years, and the set came out in 1893. He lived then in Samoa, and the isles fill his pages with heat, trade, and old rites. The set's name plays on the tale nights of the Arabian Nights.

'The Bottle Imp' is the gem of the set: a man buys a bottle with an imp that grants all wishes. The catch is grim: who dies with the bottle in hand is damned for good. The rest hold the same mix of charm, dread, and the lore of the isles.
jacobs-incidents:
Harriet Jacobs published Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl in 1861, writing under the name Linda Brent. Jacobs had escaped North years before, but she hid her identity to protect others. Hers is the classic account of slavery as a Black woman lived it.

Jacobs tells how her master harassed her from girlhood and how she resisted. To escape him she hid for seven years in a tiny crawlspace above her grandmother's porch. From there she watched her own children grow below. The book exposed slavery's assault on mothers and families to a wide Northern audience.
kelly-miller-s-history-of-the-world-war-:
Kelly Miller's History of the World War for Human Rights is a 1919 history of the Great War, copyrighted by A. Jenkins. Miller was dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at Howard University. His subtitle explains why America entered the war, states the Allies' cause, and records the part the Negro took in army and navy. Official photographs show devices of modern warfare.

Miller had written Race Adjustment, Out of the House of Bondage, and many pamphlets on social questions. Contributions came from General Pershing, Frederick Drinker, E. A. Allen, and others. The history argues that Black soldiers' service proved their claim to full American rights. It is both a war chronicle and a civil rights brief, written while the ink was fresh.
lectures-on-popular-and-scientific-subje:
The Earl of Caithness delivered these lectures on popular and scientific subjects in many places. Trübner published the second, enlarged edition in London in 1879. The Earl was a fellow of the Royal Society.

Talks treat coal and coal mines, plus science applied to art. One lecture defends thrift: take care of the pence. Others cover the steam engine and past means of travel and news. Caithness writes for general audiences, not specialists. His volume shows how Victorian lords joined the public science movement. A lecture on communication traces roads, posts, and wires. Caithness treats invention as a story for every listener.
legends-of-the-madonna-as-represented-in:
Anna Jameson wrote Legends of the Madonna as part of her Sacred and Legendary Art series. Houghton Mifflin issued this corrected, enlarged edition at Boston in 1881. Publishers note that Jameson died before revising this edition herself.

She explains how artists pictured Mary across the centuries. Paintings, sculptures, and church images guide her chapters. Stories behind the images matter as much as the art itself. Jameson helped English readers learn to read religious pictures. Her warm, learned style made art history welcoming to newcomers. Her earlier Sacred and Legendary Art volumes stand behind it. Jameson treats painters as storytellers in line and color.
legge-the-chinese-classics-vol-1-confuci:
Confucius speaks in the Analects, the heart of the first volume of Legge's Chinese Classics, printed with the Chinese text. Short sayings and brief talks with disciples fill the book. Virtue, learning, good rule, and the good life form its steady themes.

Legge's Victorian version, fruit of years in China, opened the Master to the English world. Rulers hear that kindness and rite, not force, hold a state together. Students hear that learning begins with honesty about what one knows. The Analects shaped East Asian life for two thousand years, and Legge's labor remains a monument of the field.
lollingdon-downs-and-other-poems-with-so:
John Masefield published this poetry volume with Heinemann in 1917. He dedicates the poems and sonnets to his wife. Companion volumes include Dauber, The Daffodil Fields, and Philip the King. The Faithful, a play, shares the uniform edition list.

The opening poem counts life as beads of coloured days. The self, Masefield writes, is the string holding them. Lollingdon Downs gives the collection its title and landscape. Sonnets accompany the longer poems throughout the volume. The Faithful, his play, shares the uniform volume list. Dauber and The Daffodil Fields precede Philip the King there.
macmillan-co-s-general-catalogue-of-work:
Macmillan and Co.'s General Catalogue, dated December 1869, lists their books for sale. It covers history, biography, travels, and belles lettres. Each entry carries some short account of the critical notices it won. Names here include Gladstone, Guizot, Kingsley, Freeman, and John Morley.

A publisher's catalogue is a map of what one age read. Macmillan stood among London's most respected houses in 1869. Their list mixes sermons, scholarship, novels, and tales of travel. Prices and praise helped booksellers and readers choose new works. Today the catalogue serves historians of Victorian reading. It shows the taste of a book-buying public long vanished.
maggie-a-girl-of-the-streets: Crane's 1893 Maggie follows a Bowery girl's ruin. Naturalism grinds. The Tower library holds the full text. It maggied streets. Tenements crushed. Girl fell. Pity stared. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
make-your-own-hats:
Make Your Own Hats is a millinery manual by Gene Allen Martin. Houghton Mifflin published it in 1921, with drawings by E. E. Martin. Martin directed domestic arts at the Minneapolis Y.W.C.A. She also designed and taught hat-making for many students.

The first chapters cover equipment, materials, and velvet-covered frames. Frames of neteen, crinoline, and wire each get full treatment. Later lessons turn to shaping, trimming, and finishing hats at home. The book assumes a home sewer with patience and taste. It preserves the craft behind the grand hats of 1921. Modern makers still learn from such clear, careful manuals.
marjorie-s-three-gifts:
Marjorie's Three Gifts is a short story by Louisa May Alcott. Roberts Brothers' Boston edition here dates from 1899. Marjorie sits on the doorstep shelling peas into a bright tin pan. Roses peep at her through the porch lattice, and robins wish her happy birthday.

She hears none of it, for her thoughts are far away. Last night granny told her a fairy tale of gifts. A poor girl at her spinning received a good-luck penny from a Brownie. Then a fairy passed, with a gift of her own. Alcott lets Marjorie's birthday wish meet the old tale's magic. The Little Women author writes with her usual tender wisdom.
memories-and-portraits:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathered Memories and Portraits in a set of papers. Chatto and Windus printed this fine paper edition in London in 1912. He gave the book to his mother, in past joy and present sorrow.

His note says the papers hang together more than they seem. Memories of youth and portraits of the dead build one face. That face, he found, was his own young self, long lost. He was the first to be surprised by that turn, he admits. A steamer note, written within sight of Cape Race, dates the gift. Read in order, he urges, not dipped into at random.
men-women-and-boats:
Vincent Starrett edited this posthumous collection of Stephen Crane's stories and sketches. He gathered the pieces from out-of-print books and old magazine files. Some tales appear between covers here for the first time. The title was the editor's own choice, as his note explains.

The centerpiece is The Open Boat, Crane's celebrated tale of shipwrecked men at sea. Around it stand war sketches, city pieces, and early experiments like A Dark Brown Dog. The editor regrets that copyright problems forced out The Blue Hotel. For readers, the volume recovers minor Crane works that had nearly vanished from print.
men-women-and-ghosts:
Amy Lowell's book gathers narrative poems rather than lyrics, as her preface explains. She calls them stories, stretched to the widest sense of the word. Some are tales in scenes, while others make characters of air, clouds, and streets. The poems use the free rhythms of vers libre throughout.

Lowell says Debussy's piano music showed her how movement could shape a poem. She experiments with rhythm the way a musician varies tempo and theme. Poems like A Roxbury Garden try to copy the motion of rolling hoops and growing plants. The book shows an American modernist testing what free verse could do.
mercadet-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Honoré de Balzac wrote this comedy in three acts, first staged in Paris in August 1851. The scene is a Paris house around 1845. Mercadet, a speculator, owes money to a crowd of creditors. His daughter Julie has a suitor, De la Brive, whose fortune matters greatly to the family.

Creditors like Goulard, Pierquin, and Violette press at the door from the first scene. Even the servants joke that their master is sure to drown. Mercadet schemes, stalls, and charms his way through each new demand. Balzac turns debt and speculation into fast, sharp stage comedy.
miscellaneous-mathematical-constants:
Simon Plouffe compiled this reference collection of mathematical constants at Simon Fraser University. Each number is computed to hundreds or thousands of digits. Entries range from one over pi squared, to five thousand digits, to the cosine of one at fifteen thousand digits. The file was downloaded from the Inverse Symbolic Calculator project's tables.

Named constants include Artin's, Catalan's, Champernowne's, and the Copeland-Erdos constant. Roots, exponentials, and zeta values fill out the list. The collection serves programmers and researchers who need exact digits for checking calculations. Plouffe later became known for formulas computing pi's digits, and this file shows his early precision work.
modern-religious-cults-and-movements:
Gaius Glenn Atkins, a Congregational minister and author, wrote this survey of America's new religions. His publisher's description lists the movements drawing crowds for two decades past. They include faith healing, Christian Science, and New Thought. Theosophy and spiritualism complete the set.

Atkins brought, his reviewers said, a firm grasp of Christian belief to the task. He wrote with clarity about movements many churchgoers found confusing or threatening. His other books ranged from Jerusalem's history to studies of the great mystics. This volume asks what needs the cults meet, and how the older churches should answer them.
mr-pim-passes-by-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
A. A. Milne wrote this comedy in three acts for the stage. The cast lists George Marden, his wife Olivia, and niece Dinah. Lady Marden, Brian Strange, and Carraway Pim complete the house party. The scene is the morning room at Marden House in Buckinghamshire.

Milne first staged the play in Manchester and then in London. A passing remark by Mr. Pim shakes the calm house. Old ties and young love are thrown into doubt. The mix-up is handled with light talk and neat turns. It shows Milne the playwright, years before his bear books made him most famous.
mrs-budlong-s-christmas-presents:
Rupert Hughes published this comic novel in 1912, set in the small town of Carthage. The story opens the morning after Christmas Eve. The whole house feels the ache of gifts given, missed, and received. Folks must smile and cry out that each gift is just right.

Hughes notes that Carthage folk are not rich, so gifts run small. Some are useless, and some are far too useful. Chapter titles promise schemes, foiled plans, and an amazing Christmas. Mrs. Budlong stands at the center of the giving and scheming. The book is a warm, sharp comedy about pride, love, and holiday gifts gone wrong.
music-as-a-language-lectures-to-music-st:
Ethel Home, head mistress of Kensington High School, gave these lectures to music students. Oxford's Clarendon Press issued the book in 1916. Her title claims music is a language to be taught with care. The first lecture treats the training of the music teacher.

Later lectures cover school programs, voice work, and the sol-fa method. Ear training, sight singing, rhythm, and dictation each get a chapter. She ends with harmony and first steps in composition. Home writes for teachers, not performers. Her plan shows how music was taught in British schools, step by plain step.
my-war-experiences-in-two-continents:
S. Macnaughtan's war memoir was edited by her niece after her death. John Murray issued it in London in 1919. The niece, Mrs. Lionel Salmon, shaped the letters and notes. A portrait by E. O. Hoppe fronts the volume.

The title promises war work on two continents. Macnaughtan, a novelist, went out to aid troops and the wounded. Her dedication follows a wish she had voiced herself. The book mixes letters, diary notes, and sharp witness. It shows the home front and the war zones through one tireless woman's eyes, kept in print by her family's care.
nasa-tm-19630006831-observational-astrop:
Theodore P. Stecher and James E. Milligan of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper. They gave it at the COSPAR meeting in May 1962. It reports star studies made from sounding rockets. Earth's air blocks ultraviolet light, so rockets carried the tools above it.

The paper opens by noting air is opaque below a set wavelength. Rocket flights caught ultraviolet spectra, the rainbow of starlight spread out. Observed light was checked against model stellar atmospheres. Light soaked up between the stars was part of the study. These short rocket hops opened a new window on hot stars before space telescopes flew.
nasa-tm-19650010094-scientific-explorati:
An address given on October 5, 1964, at Worcester Polytechnic Institute forms the core of this record. The speaker returned to Worcester for the institute's centennial convocation luncheon. Hugh L Dryden, NASA's deputy administrator, had been prevented from attending, the address notes.

Its subject is what the scientific exploration of space demands of education. A new field needs trained people, and schools must supply them. The speech speaks to that challenge in general terms for a general audience. It preserves how space leaders made the education case in public in 1964. Heard today, it also records the hopes and worries that space flight raised for schools at that moment.
nasa-tm-19660011717-ego-orbital-paramete:
H E Montgomery and S J Paddack, in Goddard's Theoretical Division, computed orbit data and heat inputs for the EGO satellite in April 1963. EGO was part of the Orbiting Geophysical Observatory family, called OGO in the catalog note. Their work gives orbital parameters over time, the spacecraft's changing angles, and the heat flowing into it from Sun and Earth.

Heat input decides a satellite's temperature balance in orbit. Designers need that input for each point of the path, not just an average. The authors present both their methods and their results. Other teams could then check thermal designs against real numbers, rather than rough guesses, for a large observatory satellite.
nasa-tm-19660028661-c2-swan-bands-in-com:
Ralph E. Stockhausen and Donald E. Osterbrock study comet light in this paper. Comets glow with bright bands of light from carbon molecules, called the C2 Swan bands. The authors ask how the molecules' vibration levels are populated when sunlight excites them, a process called fluorescence.

They calculate those populations two ways and get similar results. One way is a rough three-level shortcut; the other solves the balance equations for ten levels. Their excitation temperatures match published comet observations well. They also estimate the infrared glow from the same process in a bright comet, and find it small and hard to detect.
nasa-tm-19670012131-polarization-and-int:
Donald F. Heath, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1967. It reports rocket measurements of hydrogen Lyman alpha light in the day airglow, the faint ultraviolet glow of the upper atmosphere. Heath measured both the light's intensity and its polarization, a measure theorists had flagged as key to the hydrogen problem.

A far ultraviolet polarization photometer with many channels recorded intensity and polarization against altitude for several emission features. These included the Lyman alpha line, atomic oxygen lines, and an unnamed glow at longer wavelengths. The instrument flew on an Aerobee 150 rocket launched from White Sands, New Mexico, on August 29, 1966. Partner experiments on the same flight measured direct solar Lyman alpha, broadband solar flux, and electron density and temperature.
nasa-tm-19670022480-pressure-and-heat-tr:
John O. Reller Jr. and H. Lee Seegmiller, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, measured what flight does to a Mercury capsule shape. Their memorandum, TM X-647, reports pressure and heat-transfer measurements on a model of the Mercury capsule, the first American crewed spacecraft. Knowing the heating on its blunt heat shield was vital to a safe return through the atmosphere.

The program spread across three kinds of facilities: wind tunnels, shock tunnels, and free flight. Separate sections describe the models and instrumentation used in each setting. Data reduction chapters treat the calibration of the air streams, chemical equilibrium in the flow around the model. Other chapters treat heat-transfer data reduction and collected flow visualization. Results and discussion then take up the stagnation region, the heat shield, and the rest of the capsule surface in turn.
nasa-tm-19670030839-station-contact-time:
F. O. Vonbun, of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas, compiled this data paper in November 1964. It gives station contact times for Apollo orbits with variable launch azimuths. A contact time is the window during which a ground station can hear and talk to a spacecraft. Mission planners needed those windows in advance.

The paper presents graphs of contact times for the Apollo spacecraft in its parking orbits around Earth. Two orbit heights are considered, roughly two hundred and three hundred kilometers up. The graphs cover one to six parking orbits and show each ground station's windows as the launch azimuth swings across its full range. When a launch slips, the azimuth changes continuously with the delay. Vonbun hoped the graphs would help solve the tracking and communication tasks that such shifting orbits create.
nasa-tm-19680024113-variable-geometry-re:
Milton A. Beheim and Aaron S. Boksenbom of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52447, for an aeronautical sciences congress in Munich, Germany. They examine why jet inlets and exhaust nozzles for very fast aircraft must change shape in flight. A shape that works well above the speed of sound performs badly below it, they note.

Fixed shapes bring heavy pressure losses and drag at the speeds they were not built for. Lewis tests therefore compared round inlets first, with flat two-sided designs also prepared. The team varied how compression splits between outside and inside surfaces, and tried plug nozzles as well. They stress that results were still incomplete, so their conclusions stay tentative.
nasa-tm-19690010670-gamma-ray-astronomy-:
C. E. Fichtel, D. A. Kniffen, and H. B. Ogelman of Goddard Space Flight Center report gamma ray astronomy balloon results in this February 1969 paper, X-611-69-58. Balloons lift Goddard's digitized spark chamber telescope above most of the air. From that height it can catch gamma rays, the most energetic form of light, arriving from space.

The team reanalyzed data on the galactic center, hunting a possible line source in the galactic plane. Their value alone does not justify claiming a detection, they state, though it fits a satellite result. They also measured the atmospheric background glow from many angles. Upper limits on point sources fell below simple forecasts, and no positive point source evidence was found.
nasa-tm-19690030728-the-topside-ionosphe:
S. J. Bauer, R. E. Hartle, and J. R. Herman, of Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this October 1969 preprint, X-615-69-459. Their subject is the topside ionosphere of Venus and its interaction with the solar wind. Mariner V's two-frequency radio occultation experiment had watched the daytime ionosphere end abruptly. Venus has no strong magnetic shield, so the wind strikes that layer directly.

The authors picture solar wind magnetic fields piling up atop the conducting ionosphere. That magnetic obstacle, a kind of pseudo-magnetopause, raises a bow shock in the supersonic wind. Evidence came from both Mariner V and Venera IV. Using measured wind properties, they estimate the shocked gas and field buildup. Pressure balance at the cutoff, they show, fits the sharp electron density edge.
nasa-tm-19700022716-optimum-launch-traje:
Omer F. Spurlock and Fred Teren of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 astrodynamics conference in Santa Barbara, California. It finds the best launch trajectories for the ATS-E mission. ATS-E was an Applications Technology Satellite bound for a high orbit.

The authors obtained the optimum paths and present their analysis, steps, and results. Each path is computed from launch to insertion into the final orbit. Because the apogee motor was much smaller than the optimum size, the standard profile had to change. Their adjusted paths yield the greatest payload the smaller motor can deliver.
nasa-tm-19710012124-analytical-studies-o:
Theodore L. Felsentreger and James P. Murphy wrote this NASA preprint in March 1971 on luni-solar effects, the slow pulls of the Moon and Sun on artificial satellites. Those pulls gradually change a satellite's orbital elements, the numbers that describe its path. Predicting them matters for keeping spacecraft on station and for reading tracking data correctly.

The study works out perturbations in the orbital elements and compares them with effects from Earth's own gravity field. It then applies the analysis to real spacecraft: Relay 1, Telstar 2, and Relay 2. Separate sections treat shadow effects on Telstar 2, when Earth blocks the Sun's pull, and seasonal variations in Earth's gravity field. Figures track eccentricity and inclination changes for the Relay and Telstar satellites.
nasa-tm-19720017235-apollo-14-some-geoch:
Apollo 14: Some Geochemical Aspects reports the chemistry of Moon samples brought home by the Apollo 14 mission. The scan does not render its author names legibly. Apollo 14 was the first mission to visit an uplands region, away from the dark mare plains. Its landing site sat in the Fra Mauro Formation, debris thrown out by the impact that formed the Imbrium basin.

Chemical analyses covered five soil samples, three core samples, a soil clod, two breccia rocks, a basalt, and separated mineral phases. The samples proved strikingly uniform in chemistry, pointing to thorough mixing or uniform source rocks. The basalt could be matched by a mixture of about four parts soil to one part plagioclase. The authors found the samples chemically kin to Apollo 12 and 15 KREEP material, and suggested that mare basalts may represent fused cumulates.
new-arabian-nights: Stevenson's 1882 book of tales, led by the Suicide Club stories of Prince Florizel's wild nights in low London. Odd clubs, false names, and dark deeds unfold with the young writer's verve. These early pieces show him finding his voice, and they are still a pure joy to read.
night-must-fall-a-play-in-three-acts:
Emlyn Williams wrote Night Must Fall as a play in three acts, with performance rights held by his agent in London. A Lord Chief Justice appears before the play, in the Court of Criminal Appeal. The action then moves to Forest Corner, Mrs Bramson's bungalow in Essex, in the present day.

Mrs Bramson's niece Olivia Grayne and a man named Hubert Laurie join the household cast. A nurse, a cook, and a maid named Dora Parkoe fill out the house. Inspector Belsize and a man called Dan complete the list. Act one is an October morning. Act two falls twelve days later, then two days on. Crime hangs over the bungalow.
olympian-nights:
John Kendrick Bangs published this comic fantasy in 1902. Harper and Brothers issued it in New York and London. Bangs had written A House-Boat on the Styx before. The narrator reaches Mount Olympus in the first chapter. He seeks shelter among the old Greek gods.

An elevator boy and a valet serve modern comforts there. Golf links and a dining room update the ancient home. A chapter visits Aesculapius, the god of healing, as a doctor. Bangs mixes myth with modern American jokes and manners. The book is light satire for readers who know Olympus. Its humor stays playful rather than sharp.
on-nothing-kindred-subjects:
Hilaire Belloc wrote these light essays on small subjects. He dedicated the book to his friend Maurice Baring. The contents list essays on inns, ignorance, and advertisement. Other pieces treat a house, a dog, and tea. Trains, railways, and conversations in trains also appear.

Some essays turn grave, on a child who died. Others treat the return of the dead with wit. Belloc finds great truths inside trifles and daily scenes. Inns, lanes, and the human lot fill his pages. The book shows his paradoxical wisdom at play. Heads also treat a lost manuscript and a rich man's pain. A plea to take up one's pen opens the set.
pamela-giraud-a-play-in-five-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's Pamela Giraud is a play in five acts. Paris first saw it at the Théâtre de la Gaîté. The date was September 26, 1843. The scene is Paris during the Napoleonic plots. Louis the Eighteenth then reigned. The cast joins a general, a lawyer, and a wealthy merchant. Pamela herself is a poor working girl.

Act One opens in an attic and workshop. An artificial flower-maker works there by candlelight. The ceiling slopes so a man could hide behind it. Pamela sits at her work-table, discovered at her flowers. Joseph Binet sits near her. Balzac, the great novelist of money and ambition, builds his melodrama from that garret. A hidden man and a rich man's son will do the rest.
penelope-s-postscripts:
Penelope's Postscripts collects later travels of Kate Douglas Wiggin's Penelope Hamilton, in an edition published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1915. The contents list Penelope in Switzerland, in Venice, her prints of Wales, Penelope in Devon, and Penelope at home. The first piece opens in Geneva with her travelling companion Salemina.

Salemina, Penelope explains, is a charming spinster from Salem, Massachusetts, forever being asked if she is one of the P.'s of Salem. The postscripts keep the manner of the earlier Penelope books: bright letters home, full of hotels, sights, and affectionate teasing of fellow travellers.
phantom-airships-1909-1913-press-account:
Four newspaper accounts trace The Phantom Airship Waves of 1909-1913, gathered from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America. A landing reported on Caerphilly Mountain opens the British scare of 1909, when crowds scanned night skies for German raiders. An American piece blames mirages, and a Chicago aviator's supposed phantom is unmasked as himself.

The last item, from 1913, shows French troops seizing a Zeppelin at Luneville, proof of how seriously states took mystery aircraft. Together the pieces catch the mood before the First World War: new machines in the sky, old fears on the ground. They form the press record of the pre-war phantom waves.
podcast-joerogan-jYfAhupxaTs:
Rick Doblin returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1964, another lap in his long campaign. Doblin's MAPS organization had by then carried MDMA therapy through its final trials for PTSD. The finish line he had chased since the 1980s was in view.

He updates Rogan on the trial results, the regulators' questions, and what legal therapy would require of clinics. Rogan asks what could still go wrong. The episode is a hopeful progress report from the psychedelic movement's most patient man, and it pairs with his many other visits to form a full record of the cause.
political-pamphlets:
George Saintsbury edited this volume of Political Pamphlets for the Pocket Library of English Literature, published by Percival and Company in London in 1892. Saintsbury's series put short classics into portable volumes, and the pamphlet volume is a greatest-hits of English polemic: Halifax's Letter to a Dissenter, Defoe's Shortest Way with the Dissenters. The hoax that nearly got its author hanged, and Swift's Drapier's Letters, which defeated a coinage scheme and made Ireland a nation in print.

Burke's second letter on a regicide peace brings the volume to revolution, Sydney Smith's Peter Plymley letters add wit to the case for Catholic relief. Cobbett's letters to the journeymen and labourers close with radical thunder. Saintsbury, the great critical anthologist, chose pamphlets as literature, not just evidence: proof that the short prose broadside, written overnight, could outlast the books of centuries.
port-o-gold-a-history-romance-of-the-san:
Louis J. Stellman published Port o' Gold in 1922, calling it a history-romance of the San Francisco Argonauts, the forty-niners who sailed for gold. He dedicates the book to the city of his adoption and rebirth in a long poem that watches dawn break over her roofs and bay. Remembers her rising from the fiery torch, betrayed by greed and smirched by her sons' disgrace, to make herself a new and honored place.

Behind the dedication stands the whole epic: the gold discovery, the rush by sea. The instant city of gamblers, vigilantes, and dreamers, worked into fiction with real events under the plot. Stellman, a San Francisco journalist and photographer, wrote his city as romance because that is how she felt to him. The book keeps the Argonaut myth warm as the last survivors were dying.
recollections-of-bytown-and-its-old-inha:
William Pittman Lett published his recollections of Bytown and its old inhabitants at Ottawa in 1874, in verse. His introduction says the pieces began as private lines, not meant for print. Friends urged him to gather them in compact shape, and he changed his mind.

Lett states his aim plainly: to save from being lost as many names and events of Bytown's early days as memory could recall. He asks for no praise for polish of rhythm or measure, saying he aimed at truth. The town he recalls had grown, by his writing, into a city of nearly thirty thousand people.
recollections-of-the-late-william-beckfo:
Letters written by one father to his daughter preserve meetings with William Beckford of Fonthill and Lansdown, in a book taken from the 1893 edition. Charlotte Lansdown explains in a preface dated at Bath in July 1893 that her father kept the manuscript for fifty years. He meant to publish at Beckford's death in 1844 but delayed, and died sixteen years later.

Father and Beckford shared tastes, travels, and famed memories, each praising the other's recall. The first letter, dated August 21, 1838, describes Beckford's art collection in Lansdown Crescent. Its writer calls himself dazzled and drunk with beauty before the works of the great masters.
renaissance-in-italy-volume-1-of-7-the-a:
John Addington Symonds opened his seven-volume study of the Italian Renaissance with this book on the age of the despots. Henry Holt of New York issued the author's edition in 1888, dedicated to his friend John Beddoe, M.D. A line from Machiavelli's Florentine history stands in Italian at the front.

In a note to the American edition, Symonds explains his plan. The books taken together form one connected study of Italian culture at a set period. Yet each volume aims at completeness of its own and can be read alone. This first volume treats the rulers who shaped the city-states before the later volumes take up learning and art.
renaissance-in-italy-volume-3-of-7-the-f:
John Addington Symonds devoted the third volume of his Renaissance in Italy to the fine arts, in an edition from Smith, Elder of London dated 1899. A long Latin passage from Vida's Poetica stands at the front, praying that Italy always excel in the arts. Symonds states his aim plainly in the preface.

He does not retrace the whole history of Italian art, he says. He defines instead how the arts relate to the main movement of Renaissance culture. The arts began under the sway of medieval Christianity, then freed themselves step by step from church control. Their full freedom came as the classical revival reached its height.
representation-of-deities-of-the-maya-ma:
Dr. Paul Schellhas studied how gods are pictured in the Maya manuscripts, in a paper issued by the Peabody Museum of Harvard University. It forms number one of volume four of the museum's papers, in a second edition, revised. One plate and sixty-five text pictures support the study, printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in December 1904.

Selma Wesselhoeft and A. M. Parker translated the paper, and Schellhas revised their translation himself. A note explains the museum's plan: to render into English short German studies on the Maya hieroglyphs for American students. Schellhas is named there as one of the most noted scholars in the field.
rollo-at-play-or-safe-amusements:
Jacob Abbott wrote these tales of Rollo for young children, under the promise of safe amusements in the title. A notice to parents stands at the front. The first story, Rollo at Play in the Woods, follows a setting out, bridge-building, and a visitor, through a difficulty in which hearts go wrong and then right again.

The Steeple-Trap tells how to catch a squirrel, how to lose one, and how to keep one. The Halo Round the Moon brings Lucy's visit and a question of who knows best, a little boy or his father. The Freshet, Blueberrying, and Trouble on the Mountain complete the set, in small adventures with plain morals.
samuel-rutherford-and-some-of-his-corres:
Alexander Whyte, D.D., gave lectures on Samuel Rutherford and some of his correspondents in St. George's Free Church, Edinburgh, issued in 1894 by Oliphant Anderson and Ferrier. Whyte is named as author of Bunyan Characters. The first lecture is headed Joshua Redivivus, with a line from Rutherford: He sent me as a spy to see the land and to try the ford. Whyte opens by placing Rutherford's birth in the south of Scotland in the year 1600. Thomas Goodwin was born in England in the same year, he notes, with Robert Leighton, Richard Baxter, John Owen, John Bunyan, and John Howe following in later years.

A little vellum-covered volume lies open before Whyte as he speaks. Its title page reads Joshua Redivivus, or Mr.
secret-societies-and-subversive-movement:
Nesta H. Webster traced secret groups and revolt movements from old times toward her own day in this survey. Webster had already written on the French revolt and on world revolt movements. A speech by Disraeli from 1856, warning of a web of secret groups across Europe, opens the argument.

Part One covers the past: an old secret lore, revolt against Islam, the Templars, and three hundred years of occult study. Later chapters take up the start of Freemasonry and its Grand Lodge era. Webster links lodge, sect, and plot into one long chain that she holds still threatens ordered rule.
selections-from-five-english-poets:
Mary E. Litchfield edited this school volume in 1902, with an opening essay and notes on five English poets. The five are Dryden, Gray, Goldsmith, Burns, and Coleridge. Set pieces include Gray's Elegy, Goldsmith's Deserted Village, and Coleridge's Ancient Mariner.

Litchfield's Dryden essay calls him the chief writer of the late seventeenth century, a link between Milton and Pope. Dryden became poet laureate at thirty-nine, yet did his best work after fifty. Students get one famed poem or two per poet, framed by clear life sketches that place each writer in his age.
sermons-on-national-subjects:
Charles Kingsley preached these sermons on the nation's life and faith, first issued in 1880 and reprinted by Macmillan in 1890. Contents open with The King of the Earth and Holy Scripture, then move through the church year's great days. Christmas, Good Friday, Easter, and Ascension Day all appear.

Three sermons face the cholera head-on, and others treat national rewards and punishments, the covenant, and profession versus practice. Kingsley speaks to England as a parish, linking public health, war, and worship to moral law. His voice joins pulpit teaching to the pressing events of Victorian public life.
seven-men-excerpts:
Max Beerbohm published these tales in London with William Heinemann in 1919. Two tales from the full book, James Pethel and A. V. Laider, stand apart as separate files, so this copy holds the rest. Enoch Soames leads the set.

Soames, a poet of the eighteen-nineties, failed so fully that a full new book on that decade's writing leaves his name out of its index. Beerbohm notes the gap with fond cruelty. His portraits of vain, gifted, and doomed men mix pity with sharp wit, and they rank among the finest short fiction of their age.
side-lights:
James Runciman wrote these essays, issued by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1893 with a memoir by Grant Allen and an opening word by W. T. Stead. John F. Runciman edited the volume. Contents move from letter writers and the decline of literature to the surfeit of books.

Later essays treat people who are down, ill-matched and happy marriages, shrews, and the values of labor. The hopeless poor and waifs and strays close the human side of the set. Runciman writes as a journalist with a warm eye, casting side lights on the manners and strains of Victorian daily life.
sir-thomas-more-or-colloquies-on-the-pro:
Robert Southey published his colloquies with the ghost of Sir Thomas More in 1824, at age fifty, in two volumes with lake views. Cassell's 1887 printing keeps the frame while dropping a few talks whose topics had cooled. Later printings had come in 1829, 1831, and one volume in 1837.

Ghostly dialogues let Southey weigh society's progress and prospects in his later years. One famed talk shows Southey in his library, tracing the course of time through the bodies and souls of books. The editor here keeps all talks on main principles whole, for readers who want Southey's mind entire.
some-chinese-ghosts:
Lafcadio Hearn shapes old tales anew in Some Chinese Ghosts. Roberts Brothers held the 1887 copyright. Hearn gives the book to his friend Henry Edward Krehbiel. Krehbiel was a musician. In Hearn's fond account, he coaxed strange sounds from Chinese strings for him. He also won a song of their own land for Hearn. That song was the song of the jasmine flower.

Hearn's preface begs pardon for the small book. Its stuff, he says, explains its size. He sought weird beauty above all in his choices. He quotes Sir Walter Scott on things beyond sense. Such springs, Scott warned, lose their spring when pressed too hard. Readers who want Chinese letters as a whole must look past this slim set.
songs-for-parents: John Farrar wrote Songs for Parents, and his dedication gives a rhyme each to Barbara, Ted, Wink, and Dick. Dick, he jokes, is not much at reading rhymes and would rather sit and fish, but gets a couple of verses all the same. The contents sort the songs under Songs of Desire, with Summer Explorer, Spring Wish, Ambition, and Dreams, and Songs for Out of Doors, with Parade, Flower Preferences, Parental Advice, and My Garden.
stories-of-achievement-volume-iv-authors:
Volume IV of Stories of Achievement, edited by Asa Don Dickinson, turns to Authors and Journalists. Doubleday, Page and Company copyrighted the set in 1916, and this printing came from Garden City, New York, in 1925, with Robert Burns as frontispiece.

The lives run from Jean Jacques Rousseau and Burns through Charlotte Bronte, Charles Dickens, and Horace Greeley, then on to Louisa M. Alcott, Henry George, William H. Rideing, Jacob A. Riis, and Helen Keller. The contents call Rousseau the man to whom expression was travail. The volume shows young readers how writers and newsmen rose by stubborn work.
strife-a-drama-in-three-acts:
Strife, John Galsworthy's drama in three acts, prints its persons of the play at length before Act I opens in the dining room of the manager's house. John Anthony chairs the Trenartha Tin Plate Works; his son Edgar, fellow directors, the secretary Henry Tench, and manager Francis Underwood stand with the company.

Against them stand Simon Harness, a trades union official, and the workmen's committee led by David Roberts, with a crowd of men on strike behind. The wives, Annie Roberts, Mrs. Rous, and Mrs. Bulgin, are listed too, marking where the strike's hunger lands. The cast list alone frames the play's balance of boardroom, union, and home.
strong-hearts:
George W. Cable's Strong Hearts, dated 1899, holds three tales: The Solitary, The Taxidermist, and The Entomologist. The Solitary first appeared in magazine form under the title Gregory's Island, and Cable opens it with the words of Joseph reading Pharaoh's dream.

Cable speaks through a man of commerce and finance. He says the tales are one tale told several times. Each sets forth one rule in heroic natures and poetic fates. The rule is that religion without poetry is a dead thing. Poetry without religion, he adds, is just as dead. The stories test that rule on lonely, gifted people whose faith and feeling must hold together or fail.
success-with-small-fruits:
E. P. Success with Small Fruits forms Volume Seventeen of Roe's collected works. It is dated 1881 and illustrated. Roe dedicates it to his neighbor Charles Downing. Downing was a fellow horticulturist. Roe says he will count it a privilege to keep learning from him. The book teaches the growing of berries and other small fruits.

Roe's preface gives the book a second aim: to lure men and women back to their original calling, gardening. He jokes that Eve surely helped Adam in the garden and that the first pair ate small fruits at every meal and between. Every generation, he argues, can have its Eden, and many a modern Eve makes a fruitful garden with no help from Adam at all.
such-things-are-a-play-in-five-acts:
Mrs. Inchbald's Such Things Are, a play in five acts, was performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, and printed at London in a second edition dated MDCCLXXXVIII, or 1788. A prologue by Thomas Vaughan opens the volume.

Inchbald's advertisement says the subject came from the travels of an Englishman through Europe and parts of Asia to soften the sorrows of prisoners, a work of mercy that stirred wide feeling. She was uncertain where her hero was then at work. So she fixed the scene on the island of Sumatra. An English settlement stood there. Its government let the incidents keep a strict degree of probability. Benevolence, captivity, and cross-cultural encounter drive the comedy.
sword-and-crozier-drama-in-five-acts:
Indridi Einarsson's Sword and Crozier, a drama in five acts, appeared in Poet Lore in 1912 in an authorized translation from the Icelandic by Lee M. Hollander. The play is set in medieval Iceland, where bishops and chieftains fought for rule of the island.

The persons of the play name Botolf, bishop of Holar, and Kolbein Arnorsson the Young, chieftain of the North Quarter, aged thirty-four, with his wife Helga. Around them stand Kolbein Kaldaljos, the bishop's steward at seventy, his son Brand of Reynistad, a woman physician named Salvor, deacons, and henchmen on both sides. Church power and kin power meet head on, and the cast list alone shows how family ties cross the battle lines.
tales-from-the-hindu-dramatists:
R. N. Dutta, a former headmaster of the Metropolitan Institution at Calcutta and author of The Boy's Ramayana, wrote Tales from the Hindu Dramatists, printed at Calcutta by B. Banerjee and Company in 1912. J. S. Zemin, a professor of English literature and former college principal at Calcutta, revised the book.

Dutta dedicates the volume to Sir Justice Ashutosh Mookerjee. The tales retell, in plain English prose, the plots of the classical Sanskrit drama for readers who would not meet Kalidasa and his fellows in the original. Such retellings carried old stories far. They took kings, hermits, and separated lovers from the Sanskrit stage. They set them in the Indian schoolroom. They set them in the general reader's hands. The Lambs' Shakespeare did the same work at home.
tales-of-men-and-ghosts:
Edith Wharton published Tales of Men and Ghosts in London in 1910, with ten stories that mix ghost tales with sharp tales of men and money. The contents run from The Bolted Door and His Father's Son to The Eyes, Afterward, and The Letters.

The Bolted Door opens with Hubert Granice pacing his lamp-lit rooms, tense as he waits for his lawyer at eight. He dreads what the visit will seal, with no way back once the bell rings. Readers get Wharton's cool eye for fear, guilt, and pride, in tales where the ghosts may be real or may live in the mind.
tales-of-the-argonauts:
Bret Harte wrote Tales of the Argonauts, a set of tales from the California gold rush years. Contents include The Rose of Tuolumne, A Passage in the Life of Mr. John Oakhurst, Wan Lee the Pagan, and Baby Sylvester.

The Rose of Tuolumne opens late at night after a dance at Robinson's Hall, as young men ride off in all ways. One girl, loved by many, is left alone in her home at Chemisal Ridge. Readers get Harte's famed gold camp world, with gamblers, miners, and rough kindness, told in tales that helped set how the West was seen in print.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments: A contents list opens Andrew Lang's selection of The Arabian Nights Entertainments, made after the Longmans, Green and Company edition, with dates 1918 and 1898 both shown. Lang's set begins with the merchant and the genius, the fisherman, and the Greek king and the physician Douban. The three calenders and five ladies of Bagdad follow, then the seven voyages of Sindbad the Sailor. The little hunchback, the barber's fifth and sixth brothers, and Prince Camaralzaman with the Princess Badoura close the list.
the-auld-doctor-and-other-poems-and-song:
David Rorie, a doctor, gathered poems and songs written in Scots under a title that names an old doctor. An opening note explains where some pieces first appeared, in journals, student books, and song collections, and notes that one song was issued with music. Titles listed include The Lum Hat Wantin' the Croon and The Pawky Duke.

Early verses joke about a poet who has no time for lofty themes and would rather handle home topics known to doctors. The contents move from the title poem through pieces such as Macfadden and Macfee. Humour, local speech, and medical life shape the collection from its first pages.
the-automobile-girls-at-washington-or-ch:
Laura Dent Crane sent her Automobile Girls to Washington in a 1913 story about checking the plots of foreign spies. Crane is named as author of earlier books in the series set at Newport, in the Berkshires, along the Hudson, at Chicago, and at Palm Beach. A frontispiece shows a scene at the Chinese Embassy.

Chapter titles move from a chance meeting and Cabinet Day to Mr. Tu Fang Wu and a visit to the Chinese Embassy. An arrest, a White House visit, a secret errand, and a girl in danger follow. The girls uncover a confession and a tangled web before matters settle and they return home to Laurel Cottage.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-44-act:
Acts , from the King James Bible, opens by addressing Theophilus and recalling a former treatise about all Jesus began to do and teach. It runs until the day he was taken up, after giving commandments to chosen apostles.

Jesus showed himself alive after his passion by many proofs, seen for forty days, speaking of God's kingdom. Assembled with them, he commands them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father's promise. John baptized with water, he says, but they will be baptized with the Holy Ghost in a few days. They ask if the kingdom will now be restored.
the-bible-king-james-version-complete-co:
A complete King James Version text opens at Genesis, with the earth without form and void and darkness on the face of the deep. The Spirit of God moves on the face of the waters, in the numbered verse format used through the file.

God says, Let there be light, and there is light, which he sees is good. He divides light from darkness, calling light Day and darkness Night, and evening and morning are the first day. A firmament then divides waters from waters and is called Heaven. Creation in order, day by day, begins a Bible presented book by book in sequence.
the-black-cat-a-play-in-three-acts:
John Todhunter's play in three acts was first acted at the Independent Theatre in London and printed there in 1895. In a preface Todhunter questions why an author should make a speech before the curtain, except that people want views to talk about.

He records a production at the Opera Comique on December 8, 1893, for a special audience, with kind reviews. Critics objected to a tragic ending they thought tacked onto a comedy. Todhunter answers that the end was foreseen from the start and implicit in the subject. A reconciliation between husband and wife, he argues, would have been flat cynicism.
the-blue-bird-a-fairy-play-in-six-acts: Maurice Maeterlinck's fairy play in six acts, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, opens with a long list of characters. Two children, Tyltyl and Mytyl, head the list, followed by Light and the Fairy Berylune. Parents, dead grandparents, and dead brothers and sisters are all named as roles. Household things and animals also speak: Bread, Sugar, Fire, Water, Milk, a dog, and a cat. Trees, farm animals, Time, and Night complete a cast in which almost anything may take a part.
the-bores-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
The Bores is an English form of Molière's verse play Les Fâcheux, dated August 17, 1661. A long first note calls it a character play of a rare kind. Its faults on show are not held by one or two leads. They pass from one figure to the next in quick turns, each gone after a brief show. 

The note then tells how the play was made. Nicolas Fouquet, the finance chief, asked the Palais-Royal troupe for a play to amuse the King, Queen, and court at his house of Vaux-le-Vicomte. Molière had just two weeks to write it. He also had to fit in a dance by Beauchamp, a picture by Lebrun, and stage tricks by Torelli. The note praises how well he met so hard and swift a brief.
the-botanic-garden-part-2-containing-the: The Botanic Garden, Part II, holds The Loves of the Plants, a poem with notes on the thought behind the verse. This is the second form of the book, printed in London by J. Nichols for J. Johnson of St. Paul's Church Yard in 1790. A Latin motto from Claudian stands at the front. In rough sense it says leaves live for love, and palms nod to each other in bonds of love. A front plate shows Flora at play with Cupid.
the-bracelets:
Maria Edgeworth wrote The Bracelets; or, Amiability and Industry Rewarded, put out in 1850 with plates from new designs. Edgeworth had also written Popular Tales and Moral Tales. The tale is set in a fair, quiet part of England. There Mrs. Villars, a lady of clear mind, kind heart, and steady temper, keeps a school.

Twenty young folk live under her care, in full trust from their parents. Her praise is felt as the wage of merit, and her blame as the just fruit of ill acts. Each year she gives a small prize for hard work done well. This year the prize is her own portrait in a small bracelet, dear to all though it lacks gold, pearls, or gems. The two front runners are Cecilia and Leonora, close friends in an uneven way.
the-city-of-domes-a-walk-with-an-archite: John D. Barry wrote this walk with an architect about the courts of a city of domes, but only the Project Gutenberg header is present here. That header carries the standard copyright warnings, donation notes, and the Literary Archive Foundation's details.No pages of the work itself follow the front matter.
the-dark-lady-of-the-sonnets:
Bernard Shaw's The Dark Lady of the Sonnets, dated 1910, opens with a long preface. Its contents range over Thomas Tyler, Frank Harris, Shakespear's social standing, his pessimism, and the idol of the bardolaters. Shaw explains why, in this little piece written for a show aiding a National Theatre as a memorial to Shakespear, he named Mary Fitton as the Dark Lady.

He grants the case collapses on one fact: a portrait of Mary came to light showing a fair lady, not a dark one. Shakespear rubbed in the lady's dark coloring without mercy, he notes. Black hair was as unpopular then as red hair was early in Queen Victoria's reign. Any shade lighter than raven black kills the strongest claim, so Shaw gives up all pretense that his play is history.
the-easiest-way-representative-plays-by-:
Eugene Walter's play The Easiest Way heads a set of representative American plays in this printing. Walter, born in Cleveland in 1874, is quoted with rare candour. He thinks little of the play. He finds no figure in it worth much, save the old agent. He calls it photographic rather than inspired. The first audience at New York's Stuyvesant Theatre, on January 19, 1909, judged otherwise.

Crowds found its portrait of a kept woman's world harsh, true, and purging. The play's force lies in the net that closes round its heroine. It made Walter's name.
the-emancipation-of-massachusetts:
Brooks Adams's The Emancipation of Massachusetts, subtitled The Dream and the Reality, opens with thanks to friends and scholars who fed his research, among them William James. Its contents trace the colony's mind: the Commonwealth, the Antinomians, the Cambridge Platform, the Anabaptists, the Quakers, the witchcraft trials, Brattle Church, Harvard College, and the lawyers.

Adams argues that priestly rule slowly gave way to free thought in Massachusetts. His brother Henry Adams shared the theme. The book, first issued in the 1880s, stays a bold, tart read on Puritan power and its long fade.
the-fatal-boots:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The Fatal Boots as a comic tale told month by month, from January's birth of the year to December's winter of discontent. Each month heads a stage in the hero's luck.

The narrator vows that any man's true life would make a good book, then claims far more: strange, sad, unmatched adventures of his own. Yet he grants he never left his home isle nor spoke to a lord who paid his rent. The joke runs through the piece: grand boasts built on small mishaps, with a pair of boots at the root of the hero's woes.
the-folk-lore-of-plants:
T. F. Thiselton-Dyer wrote The Folk-Lore of Plants in 1889 as a brief, ordered survey of the tales and beliefs that cling to plants. His preface calls the field wide and much worked in late years.

Chapters take up plant life, early notions about plants, plant worship, lightning plants, and plants in witchcraft. Demon lore, fairy lore, and love charms follow. Thiselton-Dyer gives a few cases under each head rather than long lists, so the book serves as a handbook. A reader learns why some herbs heal in story, why some trees are feared, and how old rites live on.
the-fugitive-a-play-in-four-acts:
John Galsworthy wrote The Fugitive as a play in four acts, one of his third series of plays. Clare Dedmond, wife of George Dedmond, stands at the heart of the cast.

The cast adds Clare's brother, her friends the Fullartons, her husband's titled parents, a solicitor, a tobacconist, and a writer named Malise. The acts move from the Dedmond flat to Malise's rooms and at last to a supper room at the Gascony. Months pass between the acts. Galsworthy traces a wife who flees a cold, rich marriage and finds that flight has its own hard price.
the-gay-lord-quex-a-comedy-in-four-acts: Arthur W. Pinero wrote The Gay Lord Quex as a comedy in four acts, and only the front matter is present here. That matter lists Pinero's many plays, from The Magistrate and Dandy Dick to The Second Mrs. Tanqueray and Trelawny of the Wells, plus a note that stage rights rest with his agents, Samuel French. No cast list, scene, or speech from the comedy itself can be read in this opening portion.
the-great-adventure-a-play-of-fancy-in-f: Arnold Bennett wrote The Great Adventure. Its subtitle is A Play of Fancy in Four Acts. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a list of characters, and a list of scenes. The chief figure is Ilam Carve, an illustrious painter. The list names his valet Albert Shawn and his cousin Cyrus Carve, a city auctioneer. It names a priest, a picture dealer, and a millionaire named Texel. It names a widow, Janet Cannot. The scenes move from London to Putney. No dialogue is present.
the-hunting-of-the-snark-an-agony-in-eig: Carroll's 1876 Hunting of the Snark chases an imaginary beast in nonsense verse. The Baker vanishes. The Tower library holds the full text. It hunted nothing. Crew sailed. Snark hid. Laughter rang. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-lamp-and-the-bell-a-drama-in-five-ac: The Lamp and the Bell is a stately drama in five acts. Its characters move through passion, pride, and fate in elevated verse. The stage fills with music, shadow, and high emotion. A poetic drama for thoughtful and patient readers.
the-land-of-footprints:
Stewart Edward White published his African travel book in 1913. He opens not with his own route but with a sharp essay on books of adventure. White divides sporting writers into honest reporters and men who stretch every shot and hardship for effect.

He tells of one hunter who claimed an eland at seven hundred fifty yards. A witness later put the true range near three hundred fifty yards, still a fine shot in any honest telling. White uses the tale to promise plainer reporting about hunting, permits, and travel in little known country.
the-legends-of-king-arthur-and-his-knigh:
Sir James Knowles prepared a popular version of the Arthur legends and dedicated it to Alfred Tennyson in 1862. An addendum by Lady Knowles later explains the book long friendship with the poet. Knowles wrote that Tennyson first Idylls prompted him to seek leave for the dedication.

Tennyson praised the little book, talked Arthur with its author for years, and used it while returning to his own Arthur poem. Knowles retells the Round Table tales in plain prose for general readers. His version helped keep Malory stories in homes that found the old text hard going.
the-life-story-of-insects: Geo. H. Carpenter, professor of zoology in the Royal College of Science at Dublin, wrote his insect life story for the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature in 1913. Only the title pages and a frontispiece caption are present here, showing a gnat transformation in three stages. Larva, pupa case, and adult female appear magnified five times in that picture. The book itself, on insect growth and change for general readers, does not appear here.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1: Beyond the emperors, Suetonius also wrote brief lives of Rome's great poets — and these surviving fragments are a treasure. Virgil, Horace, Lucan, and others appear in quick, gossipy sketches full of literary anecdote. For anyone who loves classical literature, these pages offer rare glimpses of the men behind the verses.
the-mob-a-play-in-four-acts: The Mob, a play in four acts by John Galsworthy. The crowd's drama. This book preserves that play. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
the-movements-and-habits-of-climbing-pla: Darwin's 1875 book on climbing plants: how tendrils feel, grasp, and climb. Patient observation turned into science, delightful to read. The great naturalist's most charming work. Darwin's tendrils are as sensitive as fingertips, feeling their way to the sun.
the-pigeon-a-fantasy-in-three-acts: John Galsworthy's 1912 Pigeon: a fantasy of charity in three acts. Gentle and whimsical, it shows his softer side. A charming stage fantasy. Charity takes wing in Galsworthy's fantasy, a gentle stage dream, charity takes wing in fantasy.
the-pilgrims-of-hope-and-chants-for-soci: William Morris's Pilgrims of Hope and Chants for Socialists: poetry for the cause. The craftsman's socialist verse. Passionate and musical. The red poet's songs, morris sings for the socialist cause, passionate verse, musical and red, the craftsman's red songs.
the-playboy-of-the-western-world-a-comed: The Playboy of the Western World, a comedy in three acts by Synge. The boastful playboy. This book preserves that classic. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
the-queen-of-hearts: The Queen of Hearts, Wilkie Collins's story collection. The queen's tales. This book preserves that collection. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-ragged-trousered-philanthropists: Robert Tressell's The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists is a socialist classic. House painters labor for scraps while their bosses grow rich. The novel exposes the wage system with bitter humor. A landmark of working-class fiction.
the-silver-box-a-comedy-in-three-acts: John Galsworthy's 1906 Silver Box: a stolen purse exposes class justice. The play that made his name, sharp and humane. Social drama's landmark. One law for rich, one for poor, galsworthy's stage breakthrough, Galsworthy's stage breakthrough.
the-sonnets: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets, the greatest sequence in English poetry. Addressed to a beautiful young man, a dark lady, and a rival poet, they sing of love, jealousy, time, and immortality in verse of unmatched beauty. "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" is only the most famous of wonders here.
the-united-states-bill-of-rights-the-ten: The 1791 Bill of Rights lists America's first ten amendments guarding speech, arms, and trials. It limits power. The Tower library holds the full text. It chained government. Rights listed. People guarded. Freedom kept. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-well-of-the-saints-a-comedy-in-three: J. M. Synge's 1905 comedy about two blind beggars whose sight is restored, only to find the world uglier than they imagined. Bitter, funny, and poetic, it is Synge's most Swiftian play. The Abbey Theatre audience was scandalized; modern readers find it brilliant.
trevelyan-england-under-stuarts:
G. M. Trevelyan first published England under the Stuarts in 1904. Readers here meet the 1926 reprint of that lasting classic work. Seventeenth-century England, from James I to William III, fills its span.

Civil war, the republic, Restoration, and the Glorious Revolution pass in review. Trevelyan writes with grace, pace, and a liberal love of freedom. His kings and crowds live on the page in bright, quick strokes. Generations learned the Stuart age from this single, fluent volume. Its charm and clarity made dry politics read like a national novel. Trevelyan's balance of story and fact set a standard for popular history.
two-poets: Balzac's 1837 first part of Lost Illusions: two young poets in provincial Angoulême, one talented and one ambitious, dream of Paris. Lucien's vanity and David's integrity set up one of literature's great tragedies. The Human Comedy's portrait of the artist as a young man.
un-doc-initiative-on-the-safe-transporta:
The Initiative on the Safe Transportation of Grain and Foodstuffs from Ukrainian Ports was signed at Istanbul on 22 July 2022. War had shut Ukraine's Black Sea ports since February. Grain sat in silos while world food prices spiked. Türkiye, Russia, and Ukraine signed the deal, which the UN chief had proposed.

The deal opens three ports: Odesa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhny. A joint centre in Istanbul, run with the United Nations, watches each ship's path. Mixed teams in Türkiye search ships both ways for arms or stowaways. Ships move along a marked sea lane, safe from attack. The pact runs 120 days at a time and renews on its own unless a party pulls out.
uncle-vanya-scenes-from-country-life-in-: Anton Chekhov's 1899 masterpiece about wasted lives on a Russian country estate: Vanya, Sonya, and the professor's beautiful wife, all longing for what they cannot have. Quiet, devastating, and profoundly human, it is the greatest play about ordinary unhappiness.
us-constitution-bill-of-rights:
The Constitution of the United States was written at Philadelphia in 1787 and took effect in 1789. The text here adds the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791. The wording follows the edition kept by the United States House of Representatives.

The main text builds the federal government: Congress, the presidency, the courts, and the rules binding them together. It also sets how states relate to the union and how the text itself can be amended. The Bill of Rights guards speech, worship, arms, fair trials, and more against federal power. It remains the supreme law of the country.
vautrin-a-drama-in-five-acts: Balzac brings his most famous criminal — Vautrin, the escaped convict who haunts the Human Comedy — to the stage in this drama. The master manipulator schemes through Parisian society with diabolical charm. Banned in its day for its daring, the play shows Balzac's genius in theatrical form.
verses-and-sonnets: Verses and Sonnets, Hilaire Belloc's poems. The verse collection. This book preserves that poetry. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
wandering-ghosts:
F. Marion Crawford's full set of weird tales came out in 1911, the year of his death in print form here. He had writ the tales through his long life as a star of the romance world. The set holds the whole of his work in the ghost and horror kind.

'The Upper Berth' traps a man in a ship's bunk with a wet, cold thing that shares it. 'For the Blood Is the Life' is a vampire tale of Italy, and 'The Screaming Skull' a tale of a skull that will not rest. The set is the one book to own for Crawford's ghost craft.
